Small
smȧl
adj. (little in size, number, or degree; rendering Hebrew qatan, daq, Greek mikros)
From Saxon smæl, slender or narrow. Scripture attaches enormous weight to small things — a still small voice, a day of small things, a very small helm — because God's method is regularly to work by what men would overlook.

Biblical Definition

Small in Scripture is rarely a dismissal. At Horeb the LORD passes by in wind, earthquake, and fire, and is in none of them; what remains is “a still small voice” (1 Kings 19:12), and that is where God is. The prophet had asked for vindication by spectacle and was answered by the opposite. Zechariah rebukes the contempt directly, and does so while a half-built temple stood as the evidence: “For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth” (Zechariah 4:10). The plummet in a builder's hand is a small sight, and the eyes of the LORD are upon it. Job's counsellor states the general rule of God's way with beginnings: “Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase” (Job 8:7). Small is also a diagnostic word, and one proverb turns it upon the man himself with disconcerting economy: “If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small” (Proverbs 24:10). Adversity does not create the smallness; it measures it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Slender; thin; little in size, quantity, degree, or importance. Scripture invests small things with weight — the still small voice, the day of small things, the small beginning — and uses smallness of strength as a diagnosis revealed by adversity.

expand to see more

SMALL, a. [Sax. smæl; G. schmal, narrow.] Slender; thin; fine; of little diameter; hence, in general, little in size or quantity.

2. Minute; slight; as, a small effort; a small matter.

3. Little in degree; as, small progress.

4. Being of little moment, weight or importance; as, it is a small matter.

5. Not loud; soft; gentle; as, a small voice.

6. Narrow; as, the small of the leg or back. SMALLNESS, n. Littleness of size, quantity, or importance.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 19:12 — "And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice."

Zechariah 4:10 — "For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth."

Job 8:7 — "Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase."

Proverbs 24:10 — "If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small."

Modern Corruption

Scale has become the measure of divine approval, so that the day of small things is despised in practice by a church that reckons faithfulness by size and treats the still small voice as a stage in the story rather than the point of it.

expand to see more

Zechariah's question is not rhetorical decoration; it was addressed to men who had seen the first temple and wept at the second. The despising of small things is a permanent religious temptation, and it is now institutionalized. Ministries are assessed by attendance, reach, and growth curves, and a faithful congregation of eighty is quietly classed as a problem to be solved. Scripture's own accounting is different: the plummet in Zerubbabel's hand is watched by the eyes of the LORD which run to and fro through the whole earth. What is small is not therefore unobserved; it is observed by the only Eyes whose assessment is final.

The parallel error is to seek God in the spectacular and to miss Him in the ordinary means. Elijah at Horeb is the standing rebuke. Wind, earthquake, and fire pass, and the LORD is in none of them; the word comes in a still small voice. A religion of dramatic signs and continuing revelations repeats the prophet's mistake with none of his excuse, since the canon is closed and the ordinary means — the word preached, the ordinances, prayer — are precisely the small things God has appointed. Recover the pattern, and smallness stops being a discouragement and becomes a category of expectation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qatan (small, young, insignificant) and daq (thin, fine) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek mikros (small, little) and elachistos (least) carry them into the New.

expand to see more

Hebrew qatan (H6996) — small, little, young; the word of Zechariah's “day of small things”.

Hebrew daq (H1851) — thin, fine, small; used of the fine dust and of the still small voice at Horeb.

Hebrew demamah (H1827) — a whisper, a calm stillness; joined to daq in 1 Kings 19:12.

Greek mikros (G3398) — small, little; used of the mustard seed and of the little ones who believe.

Greek elachistos (G1646) — least, smallest; the measure of faithfulness in our Lord's parable of the talents.

Usage

"“A still small voice” — God was in what the spectacle had passed over."

"“Who hath despised the day of small things?” — the question rebukes a permanent temptation."

"“If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small” — trouble measures strength rather than creating weakness."
